topics.title: What a computer is: the block diagram

learn.hook: When you tap 'Book' on the IRCTC app, a chain of input, processing, storage and output fires in well under a second. That chain is the block diagram of every computer.
points: A computer is an electronic device that accepts data (input), processes it according to a set of instructions (a program) and produces results (output).
Block diagram: Input unit → CPU (with memory) → Output unit, with secondary storage holding data and programs permanently. Data and instructions travel between these units.
The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the 'brain'. It has three parts: the ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit), the CU (Control Unit) and registers.
ALU: does arithmetic (+, −, ×, ÷) and logical work (comparisons such as >, <, =). CU: fetches and decodes instructions and directs every other unit, like a traffic controller.
Registers: tiny, very fast storage cells inside the CPU that hold the data and instructions being worked on right now.

example.q: A student types 45 + 30 on a calculator app and sees 75. Trace the path through the block diagram.
steps: Input unit: the touch screen sends 45, +, 30 to the computer as binary.
Memory: the numbers and the instruction are held in primary memory (RAM).
CU: fetches the 'add' instruction and tells the ALU what to do; the operands sit in registers.
ALU: adds them to get 75 and the result goes back to a register/memory.
Output unit: the screen displays 75.
example.answer: Input → memory → CU directs → ALU computes → output

learn.reallife: ISRO's mission computers at Sriharikota take sensor input from the rocket, process it in real time and output commands to the engines: the same input-process-output cycle, at very high speed.

games.title: Unit ↔ its job
pairs: Directs and coordinates all other units
Hold data the CPU is using right now

games.title: Data's journey
games.prompt: Put the stages of processing in order
items: Data entered through an input device
Control Unit fetches and decodes the instruction
Result shown on an output device

quiz.q: Which part of the CPU decides whether 'marks >= 33' is True?
quiz.explain: Comparisons are logical operations, and logical operations are done by the ALU.
steps: 'marks >= 33' is a comparison
Comparisons are logical operations
Logical operations are done by the ALU
Answer: Arithmetic Logic Unit
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Control Unit makes decisions, when it only directs the ALU

quiz.q: Which part of the CPU fetches an instruction, decodes it and signals the other units?
quiz.explain: The CU manages and coordinates: it fetches, decodes and issues control signals. It does not compute results itself.
steps: Fetching, decoding and signalling other units is coordination work
The CPU part that coordinates is the Control Unit
The ALU only computes
Answer: Control Unit
quiz.mistake: Confuses directing work (CU) with doing arithmetic (ALU)

quiz.q: Registers are best described as:
options: Small, high-speed storage locations inside the CPU
quiz.explain: Registers sit inside the CPU and temporarily hold the data and instructions being processed. They are the fastest memory.
steps: Registers sit inside the CPU
They hold the data and instructions being worked on right now
They are small and the fastest memory
Answer: Small, high-speed storage locations inside the CPU
quiz.mistake: Mixes registers with secondary storage because both 'store' data

quiz.q: Which statement correctly defines a computer?
options: A device that stores data but cannot process it
An electronic device that takes input, processes it under the control of instructions and gives output
A machine that can only perform arithmetic
Any device that runs on electricity
quiz.explain: A computer is defined by input, processing under program control, and output. Arithmetic alone or storage alone is not enough.
steps: A computer must take input, process it under instructions, and give output
Storage alone or arithmetic alone is not enough
Not every electric device is a computer
Answer: An electronic device that takes input, processes it under the control of instructions and gives output
quiz.mistake: Picks a definition that captures only one function of a computer

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The CPU is called the brain of the computer.
Reason (R): The CPU carries out instructions and controls the working of all other units.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: The CPU executes instructions (via the ALU) and controls other units (via the CU), which is exactly why it is called the brain.
steps: A: the CPU is called the brain — true
R: it carries out instructions and controls all other units — true, and that is exactly why it is called the brain
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link the reason to the assertion

quiz.q: In the block diagram, where are the program and data kept while the CPU is working on them?
quiz.explain: The CPU reads instructions and data from primary memory while processing. Input and output units only bring data in or send it out.
steps: While working, the CPU reads instructions and data from primary memory
Input and output units only bring data in or send it out
So they are kept in primary memory (RAM)
Answer: Primary memory (RAM)
quiz.mistake: Thinks data stays inside the input device until processed

quiz.q: Which pair of units together form the CPU's processing core along with registers?
quiz.explain: The CPU consists of the ALU, the CU and registers. RAM and hard disk are memory/storage outside the CPU.
steps: The CPU consists of the ALU, the Control Unit and registers
RAM and hard disk are memory outside the CPU
So the pair is the ALU and the Control Unit
Answer: ALU and Control Unit
quiz.mistake: Counts memory chips as parts of the CPU

quiz.q: Case: A self-service railway ticket kiosk at a station reads your touch selection, computes the fare and prints the ticket. Which is the correct sequence of units used?
quiz.explain: Data first enters through an input device, is processed by the CPU, and the result is sent to an output device.
steps: The touch selection enters first (input)
The fare is computed (CPU)
The ticket is printed (output)
Answer: Input (touch screen) → CPU → Output (printer)
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the direction of data flow

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know what happens inside a computer between pressing a key and seeing the result. Explain the block diagram and the parts of the CPU.
teach.praise: Brilliant! Input, CPU with ALU and CU, then output — I can see the whole pipeline now!
teach.nudge: You've got part of it. Who does the arithmetic and who directs the other units inside the CPU?

revise.summary: A computer is an electronic device that takes input, processes it under the control of a program and gives output. Its CPU has the ALU (arithmetic and logic), the Control Unit (fetches, decodes, directs) and registers (tiny, fast storage), working with memory.
focus: Draw and explain the block diagram: input → CPU (with memory) → output
State the jobs of the ALU, the Control Unit and registers
Trace a task through the units in the right order
remember: Computer: accepts input, processes it under program control, produces output
ALU: arithmetic (+, −, ×, ÷) and logic (comparisons like >, <, =)
CU: fetches and decodes instructions and directs all other units
Registers: small, very fast storage inside the CPU
traps: Comparisons such as marks >= 33 are done by the ALU, not the CU
RAM and the hard disk are outside the CPU; the CPU is ALU + CU + registers

topics.title: Input devices, output devices and kinds of computers

learn.hook: Your Aadhaar fingerprint scan, your school's smartboard and the token-number speaker at a bank are all I/O devices doing one job each.
points: Input devices convert data from the outside world into a form the computer can process: keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, touch screen, webcam, and biometric sensors such as fingerprint or iris scanners.
Output devices convert processed data into a form people can use: monitor, printer, speaker, projector, and 3D printer (which builds a solid object layer by layer).
A touch screen works as both an input device (you tap) and an output device (it displays).
Hardware is the physical part you can touch (CPU, keyboard, monitor). Software is the set of programs that tells the hardware what to do.
Computers come in many forms: servers, desktops, laptops, tablets and smartphones. All follow the same input-process-output idea.

example.q: Classify for a bank: cheque scanner, passbook printer, PIN keypad, display board.
steps: Ask: does the device bring data IN or send results OUT?
Cheque scanner reads the cheque → input
PIN keypad sends digits → input
Passbook printer prints entries → output
Display board shows token numbers → output
example.answer: Input: scanner, keypad. Output: printer, display board.

learn.reallife: Aadhaar-based attendance in many government offices uses a fingerprint scanner (input), a server that matches the print (processing) and a screen or SMS confirming attendance (output).

games.title: Hardware or not?
items: A device driver is a piece of hardware.
A device driver is software that lets the OS talk to a hardware device.
A touch screen can act as both input and output device.
You give input by touching it and it displays output.
It takes input, processes it with a processor under program control and gives output.
A 3D printer is an input device.
It creates physical objects from a digital design, so it is an output device.
Software is a set of instructions; only the medium storing it is physical.

quiz.q: Which of these is an output device?
quiz.explain: A projector displays processed data on a screen. The others send data into the computer.
steps: Output devices show processed data to people
A projector displays it on a screen
Scanners, microphones and biometric sensors send data in
Answer: Projector
quiz.mistake: Treats any device attached to a computer as output

quiz.q: A doctor at AIIMS dictates notes into speech-to-text software. Which input device is used?
quiz.explain: A microphone captures sound and converts it to digital data, so it is an input device.
steps: The doctor's voice must go into the computer
A microphone captures sound and converts it to digital data
So the input device is the microphone
Answer: Microphone
quiz.mistake: Confuses the microphone (input) with the speaker (output)

quiz.q: Which device can work as both an input and an output device?
quiz.explain: A touch screen displays information and also senses your touch.
steps: A touch screen displays information (output)
and also senses your touch (input)
So it works as both
Answer: Touch screen
quiz.mistake: Picks a device that does only one of the two jobs

quiz.q: Which one of the following is software, not hardware?
quiz.explain: An operating system is a set of programs. The others are physical components.
steps: Hardware is physical: motherboard, keyboard, RAM chip
An operating system is a set of programs
So the operating system is software
Answer: Operating system
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything inside the cabinet must be hardware

quiz.q: What does a 3D printer produce?
options: A scanned image of an object
A solid three-dimensional object built layer by layer
quiz.explain: A 3D printer is an output device that builds physical objects from a digital design, layer upon layer.
steps: A 3D printer is an output device
It builds a solid object from a digital design
layer by layer
Answer: A solid three-dimensional object built layer by layer
quiz.mistake: Thinks 3D printing is just colour printing

quiz.q: A shop uses a barcode reader at the billing counter. The barcode reader is:
quiz.explain: It reads the code on the product and sends it into the computer, which is input.
steps: The barcode reader reads the product code
and sends it into the computer
That makes it an input device
Answer: An input device
quiz.mistake: Thinks the device that 'reads' shows output

quiz.q: Which statement about different computers is correct?
options: Servers, laptops and smartphones all work on the input-process-output principle
quiz.explain: Every type of computer, from a server to a phone, takes input, processes it and produces output.
steps: Servers, laptops and smartphones all take input
process it and produce output
So they all follow the input-process-output principle
Answer: Servers, laptops and smartphones all work on the input-process-output principle
quiz.mistake: Thinks only big desk machines count as computers

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A speaker is an output device.
Reason (R): A speaker converts digital audio signals from the computer into sound.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: A speaker turns processed digital data into sound for us, which is exactly what makes it an output device.
steps: A: a speaker is an output device — true
R: it converts digital audio from the computer into sound — true, and that is what makes it an output device
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Misses that R gives the reason for A

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'Is a scanner input or output? And what is hardware versus software?' Help Gappu out.
teach.praise: Now I can sort every gadget on my desk! Hardware I can touch, software I can't, and devices either bring data in or send it out.
teach.nudge: Nice start. Can you also say which devices bring data in, which send results out, and what hardware vs software means?

revise.summary: Input devices bring data into the computer (keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, biometric sensors); output devices present results (monitor, printer, speaker, projector, 3D printer). A touch screen does both. Hardware is physical; software is the programs that run it.
focus: Classify devices as input, output or both
Tell hardware from software
Explain that all kinds of computers follow input-process-output
remember: Input: keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, touch screen, webcam, biometric sensors, barcode reader
Output: monitor, printer, speaker, projector, 3D printer
Touch screen: both input and output
Hardware: physical parts; software: programs that tell the hardware what to do
traps: A scanner or barcode reader is input, not output
An operating system is software, not hardware

learn.hook: The phone in your pocket is millions of times more powerful than the room-sized machines of the 1940s. How did we get from beads on wires to AI chips?
points: Early aids: the abacus (beads on rods for counting), Blaise Pascal's Pascaline (1642, a mechanical adding machine) and Leibniz's Stepped Reckoner, which could also multiply and divide.

Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine (1834), a mechanical general-purpose machine with a 'mill' (processing) and a 'store' (memory): the first idea of a programmable computer. Herman Hollerith used punched cards to process the 1890 US census.
John von Neumann's stored-program architecture: the program and data are both kept in the same memory, and the CPU fetches instructions one by one. Almost all modern computers follow it.

Generations: 1st – vacuum tubes; 2nd – transistors; 3rd – integrated circuits (ICs); 4th – VLSI microprocessors; 5th – usually described as computers built around artificial intelligence, using ULSI (Ultra Large Scale Integration) chips.
Personal computers, laptops and smartphones followed microprocessors. Today's trends include wearables, the Internet of Things (IoT) and artificial intelligence (AI).

example.q: Arrange: transistor-based computer, abacus, smart watch, Analytical Engine, vacuum-tube computer.
steps: Abacus: ancient counting aid
Analytical Engine: 1830s design by Babbage
Vacuum-tube computer: first generation (1940s)
Transistor-based computer: second generation
Smart watch: today's wearable computer
example.answer: Abacus → Analytical Engine → vacuum tubes → transistors → smart watch

learn.reallife: India's own PARAM 8000 supercomputer (C-DAC, 1991) and today's AI-powered UPI fraud checks show how computing grew from big machines to everyday intelligent systems.

quiz.q: Which technology defines second-generation computers?
quiz.explain: Transistors replaced vacuum tubes in the second generation, making computers smaller and more reliable.
steps: 1st generation used vacuum tubes
Transistors replaced them in the 2nd generation
ICs and VLSI came later
Answer: Transistors
quiz.mistake: Shifts the generations by one

quiz.q: The stored-program concept, where both program and data are kept in memory, is credited to:
quiz.explain: Von Neumann's architecture keeps instructions and data together in memory. Modern computers still follow it.
steps: Keeping both the program and its data in the same memory
is the stored-program concept
It is credited to John von Neumann
Answer: John von Neumann
quiz.mistake: Credits Babbage because he designed an early programmable machine

quiz.q: Who is known for designing the Analytical Engine, the first concept of a general-purpose programmable computer?
quiz.explain: Babbage's Analytical Engine (1834) had a mill and a store and could follow instructions on punched cards.
steps: The Analytical Engine (1834) had a mill and a store
and could follow instructions on punched cards
It was designed by Charles Babbage
Answer: Charles Babbage
quiz.mistake: Mixes up early calculator inventors with Babbage

quiz.q: Herman Hollerith's major contribution was:
options: Using punched cards to tabulate census data
quiz.explain: Hollerith's tabulating machine read punched cards and processed the 1890 US census much faster.
steps: Hollerith built a tabulating machine that read punched cards
It processed the 1890 US census much faster
So his contribution was using punched cards for census data
Answer: Using punched cards to tabulate census data
quiz.mistake: Links Hollerith to the wrong invention

quiz.q: Which was mainly an adding machine built in 1642?
quiz.explain: Blaise Pascal built the Pascaline in 1642 to add and subtract mechanically.
steps: Blaise Pascal built a mechanical adding machine in 1642
It could add and subtract
That was the Pascaline
Answer: Pascaline
quiz.mistake: Confuses Pascal's and Leibniz's machines

quiz.q: Fourth-generation computers are based on:
quiz.explain: Very Large Scale Integration put an entire CPU on one chip, the microprocessor, giving us personal computers.
steps: VLSI put a whole CPU on one chip, the microprocessor
That defines the 4th generation
Vacuum tubes and transistors were earlier
Answer: VLSI microprocessors
quiz.mistake: Thinks ICs and VLSI belong to the same generation

quiz.q: Smart watches and fitness bands that send data to a phone are examples of:
options: Wearable devices, part of the IoT trend
quiz.explain: Wearables are small computers worn on the body, and when connected they are part of the Internet of Things.
steps: Smart watches and fitness bands are worn on the body
and connected to a phone
They are wearables, part of the IoT trend
Answer: Wearable devices, part of the IoT trend
quiz.mistake: Does not link small gadgets with being computers

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): First-generation computers were very large and produced a lot of heat.
Reason (R): They used thousands of vacuum tubes.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Vacuum tubes were bulky and hot, so machines using thousands of them were huge and heat-producing.
steps: A: 1st-generation computers were huge and hot — true
R: they used thousands of vacuum tubes — true, and bulky, hot tubes explain A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Treats two true statements as unrelated

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Were computers always this small?' Explain how computers evolved from early machines through the generations.
teach.praise: Wow, from beads to vacuum tubes to tiny chips! I'll never look at my phone the same way.
teach.nudge: Good! But what technology did each generation use — vacuum tubes, then what?

revise.summary: Computing grew from the abacus, Pascal's Pascaline (1642) and Leibniz's Stepped Reckoner to Babbage's Analytical Engine (1834) and Hollerith's punched cards. Von Neumann's stored-program idea underlies modern computers, whose generations used vacuum tubes, transistors, ICs, VLSI and AI.
focus: Match inventors and machines in the history of computing
Recall the technology of each computer generation
Explain the stored-program concept
Recognise modern trends: wearables, IoT, AI
remember: Pascaline (1642): mechanical adding machine; Analytical Engine (1834, Babbage): mill + store, programmable
Hollerith: punched cards for the 1890 US census
Von Neumann: program and data stored together in memory
Generations: 1st vacuum tubes, 2nd transistors, 3rd ICs, 4th VLSI microprocessors, 5th AI with ULSI
traps: Transistors are 2nd generation; vacuum tubes are 1st
The stored-program concept is von Neumann's, not Babbage's

topics.title: Why memory matters and units of memory

learn.hook: A 4K movie is about 20 GB, but a WhatsApp text is only a few bytes. Knowing memory units helps you guess what fits in your phone.
points: A computer needs memory to hold the data being processed, the instructions (program) and the results. Without memory the CPU would have nothing to work on.
Bit (binary digit, 0 or 1) is the smallest unit. 4 bits = 1 nibble. 8 bits = 1 byte.
1 KB (kilobyte) = 1024 bytes; 1 MB = 1024 KB; 1 GB = 1024 MB; 1 TB = 1024 GB; 1 PB = 1024 TB. Each step is 2¹⁰ = 1024.
To go to a smaller unit, multiply by 1024; to go to a bigger unit, divide by 1024. Bits ↔ bytes uses 8.

example.q: How many bits are in 2 KB?
steps: 2 KB = 2 × 1024 bytes = 2048 bytes
1 byte = 8 bits

learn.reallife: An ISRO satellite downlinking 1 TB of imagery a day is sending 1024 × 1024 MB: that is why ground stations need huge storage farms.

games.title: Smallest to largest
games.prompt: Arrange the memory units from smallest to largest

quiz.q: How many megabytes are there in 4 GB?
steps: 1 GB = 1024 MB
Answer: 4096
quiz.mistake: Uses 1000 instead of 1024

quiz.q: A file is 8192 bytes. What is its size in KB?
quiz.explain: Divide by 1024 to go from bytes to KB: 8192 ÷ 1024 = 8 KB.
steps: Bytes → KB: divide by 1024
Answer: 8
quiz.mistake: Divides by 1000 instead of 1024

quiz.q: How many bits are there in 3 bytes?
quiz.explain: 1 byte = 8 bits, so 3 bytes = 24 bits.
steps: 1 byte = 8 bits
Answer: 24
quiz.mistake: Uses 4 bits per byte (confusing a byte with a nibble)

quiz.q: How many nibbles make 1 KB?
quiz.explain: 1 KB = 1024 bytes and each byte has 2 nibbles, so 1024 × 2 = 2048 nibbles.
steps: 1 KB = 1024 bytes
1 byte = 2 nibbles
Answer: 2048
quiz.mistake: Forgets that a byte has two nibbles

quiz.q: Which is the correct ascending order of memory units?
options: Byte < KB < GB < MB < TB < PB
Byte < KB < MB < GB < TB < PB
KB < Byte < MB < GB < TB < PB
Byte < MB < KB < GB < PB < TB
quiz.explain: Each unit is 1024 times the previous: byte, KB, MB, GB, TB, PB.
steps: Each unit is 1024 times the one before
Byte, then KB, MB, GB, TB, PB
So Byte < KB < MB < GB < TB < PB
Answer: Byte < KB < MB < GB < TB < PB
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of MB and GB or TB and PB

quiz.q: A phone has 128 GB storage. How many such phones together hold 1 TB?
steps: 1 TB = 1024 GB
Answer: 8
quiz.mistake: Uses 1 TB = 1000 GB and gets a non-whole number

quiz.q: Why does a computer need memory at all?
options: To hold the data, instructions and results the CPU works with
Only to connect to the internet
Only to store movies and photos
quiz.explain: The CPU can only process what is in memory: the instructions to follow and the data to work on.
steps: The CPU can only work on what is in memory
Memory holds the instructions, the data and the results
So it is needed to hold the data, instructions and results the CPU works with
Answer: To hold the data, instructions and results the CPU works with
quiz.mistake: Thinks memory is only for saving personal files

quiz.q: How many bytes are there in 2 MB?
steps: Answer: 2097152
quiz.mistake: Stops at KB or uses powers of 1000

teach.ask: Gappu wonders, 'Why does a computer need memory, and how big is a kilobyte?' Explain memory and its units.
teach.praise: So a byte is 8 bits and every step up is 1024 times bigger. Memory maths makes sense now!
teach.nudge: Almost there! How many bits make a byte, and what number do we multiply by to go from KB to bytes?

revise.summary: A computer needs memory to hold data, instructions and results. The bit is the smallest unit; 4 bits make a nibble and 8 bits a byte. Each larger unit is 1024 times the previous: KB, MB, GB, TB, PB.
focus: Convert between bits, bytes and larger units
Order memory units correctly
Explain why memory is needed
remember: 1 nibble = 4 bits; 1 byte = 8 bits
1 KB = 1024 bytes; 1 MB = 1024 KB; 1 GB = 1024 MB; 1 TB = 1024 GB; 1 PB = 1024 TB
Smaller unit: multiply by 1024; bigger unit: divide by 1024; bits ↔ bytes uses 8
traps: MB comes before GB: Byte < KB < MB < GB < TB < PB
Each step is 1024, not 1000, in this chapter

topics.title: Types of memory: RAM, ROM, cache and secondary storage

learn.hook: Your laptop forgets unsaved work when the power cuts, yet still knows how to start up. Two different memories are at play.
points: Primary memory is directly accessed by the CPU. RAM (Random Access Memory) is read-write and volatile: its contents are lost when power goes off. It holds running programs and data.
ROM (Read Only Memory) is non-volatile: it keeps its contents without power. It stores start-up (boot) instructions, such as the BIOS/firmware.
Cache memory is a small, very fast memory placed between the CPU and RAM. It keeps frequently used data and instructions so the CPU does not wait for slower RAM.
Secondary memory is non-volatile, larger, cheaper per GB and slower: HDD, SSD, CD/DVD, pen drive, memory card. It stores data permanently but the CPU cannot access it directly.
Memory hierarchy (fastest/costliest/smallest → slowest/cheapest/largest): registers → cache → RAM → secondary storage.

example.q: A student's laptop restarts after a power cut. Which work is lost, and which instructions let it start again?
steps: The open, unsaved document was in RAM
RAM is volatile, so it was erased when power was lost
Boot instructions are stored in ROM, which is non-volatile
Saved files on the SSD (secondary memory) are safe
example.answer: Unsaved work in RAM is lost; ROM's boot instructions and SSD files survive.

learn.reallife: At a busy Indian Railways reservation server, the most-used route and fare data are kept in cache and RAM for speed, while years of booking records live on large secondary storage.

quiz.q: Which memory loses its contents when the power is switched off?
quiz.explain: RAM is volatile, so it needs power to keep data.
steps: Volatile memory needs power to keep its data
RAM is volatile
ROM, hard disks and pen drives keep data without power
Answer: RAM
quiz.mistake: Thinks all primary memory is volatile, including ROM

quiz.q: Where are the instructions needed to start up (boot) a computer usually stored?
quiz.explain: ROM is non-volatile, so boot instructions remain available every time the computer is switched on.
steps: Boot instructions must be ready every time the computer starts
So they are kept in non-volatile memory
That is ROM
Answer: ROM
quiz.mistake: Thinks boot instructions are in RAM, which is empty at power-on

quiz.q: Cache memory is placed between:
quiz.explain: Cache is a small, fast buffer between the CPU and main memory that holds frequently used data.
steps: Cache is a small, fast buffer
that holds frequently used data close to the CPU
It sits between the CPU and RAM
Answer: The CPU and RAM
quiz.mistake: Places cache between RAM and secondary storage

quiz.q: Compared with primary memory, secondary memory is:
options: Directly used by the ALU for every calculation
quiz.explain: Secondary storage trades speed for large, cheap, permanent capacity.
steps: Secondary storage trades speed for capacity
It is slower, larger and non-volatile
and cheaper per GB
Answer: Slower, larger and non-volatile
quiz.mistake: Assumes bigger storage must also be faster

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a secondary storage device?
quiz.explain: RAM is primary memory. SSDs, memory cards and DVDs store data permanently as secondary storage.
steps: SSDs, memory cards and DVDs store data permanently
RAM is primary memory
So RAM is NOT secondary storage
Answer: RAM
quiz.mistake: Thinks RAM is storage because people say 'memory' for both

quiz.q: Arrange from fastest to slowest: RAM, registers, hard disk, cache.
quiz.explain: Registers are inside the CPU and fastest, then cache, then RAM, and the hard disk is slowest.
steps: Registers are inside the CPU and fastest
then cache, then RAM
and the hard disk is slowest
Answer: Registers, cache, RAM, hard disk
quiz.mistake: Puts cache before registers

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The CPU keeps frequently used data in cache memory.
Reason (R): Cache is faster than RAM.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Because cache is faster than RAM, keeping frequently used data there reduces the time the CPU waits.
steps: A: the CPU keeps frequently used data in cache — true
R: cache is faster than RAM — true, and that is why it reduces the CPU's waiting time
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Doesn't see that speed is the reason for using cache

quiz.q: A student says, 'ROM is read-only, so it is volatile.' What is wrong?
options: ROM is non-volatile: it keeps data without power
quiz.explain: 'Read-only' is about not writing normally; 'volatile' is about losing data without power. ROM keeps its data.
steps: 'Read-only' means it is not normally written to
'Volatile' means losing data without power
Answer: ROM is non-volatile: it keeps data without power
quiz.mistake: Confuses the idea of read-only with volatility

teach.ask: Gappu's tablet lost his unsaved drawing in a power cut but still turned on. Explain RAM, ROM, cache and secondary memory to him.

learn.hook: Inside your laptop, data races along tiny copper highways at billions of cycles per second. Which highway carries what?
points: The system bus is a set of wires that carries data, addresses and control signals between the CPU, memory and I/O devices.

Data bus: carries the actual data; it is bidirectional (data moves to and from the CPU). Address bus: carries the memory address the CPU wants; it is unidirectional (CPU → memory). Control bus: carries control signals such as read/write and timing.
A microprocessor is a CPU built on a single chip. Intel's 4004 (1971) was 4-bit; today's chips are 64-bit and multi-core (dual-core, quad-core, octa-core).

Specifications: word size (bits processed at once, e.g. 64-bit), memory size (how much memory it can address; with 32 address bits, 2³² bytes = 4 GB), clock speed (cycles per second, in Hz/GHz) and number of cores.
A microcontroller is a small computer on one chip, with CPU, memory and I/O ports, built for one dedicated job in embedded devices: washing machines, microwave ovens, TV remotes.

example.q: A processor can use 32 address bits. What is the largest memory it can address, in GB?
steps: Number of addresses = 2³²
2³² bytes = 2² × 2³⁰ bytes
2³⁰ bytes = 1 GB
So 2² GB = 4 GB

learn.reallife: The smart electricity meters being installed across Indian cities contain microcontrollers that read consumption and send it to the DISCOM, while your phone uses an octa-core microprocessor.

learn.hook: '98, 87, 91' means nothing. 'Priya's average is 92' means a lot. That jump from data to information is what computers are for.
points: Data are raw, unorganised facts (numbers, text, images). Information is data processed into a meaningful, useful form.

Structured data follows a fixed format, like rows and columns in a table (a marks register). Unstructured data has no fixed format (photos, audio, video, free text posts). Semi-structured data has some organisation through tags but not a strict table (emails, HTML, XML files).
Data capturing collects data through input devices or sensors; data storage keeps it on storage media; data retrieval fetches stored data when needed.

Deleting a file usually moves it to the Recycle Bin; even after emptying it, the data often stays on the disk until overwritten. Recovery tools can bring it back, which is useful but also a privacy risk when old devices are sold.

steps: Spreadsheet: fixed rows and columns → structured
CCTV video: no row/column format → unstructured

learn.hook: The CPU understands only 0s and 1s, yet you write print('Hello'). Who translates?
points: Hardware does nothing on its own; software (a set of programs) gives it instructions. Software is broadly system software, programming tools and application software.

System software runs the computer itself: the operating system, system utilities (antivirus, disk cleanup, backup, compression) and device drivers (let the OS control a particular device such as a printer).

Low-level languages: machine language (binary 0s and 1s, directly understood by the CPU) and assembly language (mnemonics like ADD, MOV). High-level languages (Python, C++, Java) are close to English and portable.

Translators: an assembler converts assembly to machine code. A compiler translates the whole program at once and lists errors after scanning it. An interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time and stops at the first error. Python uses an interpreter.
Program development tools: text editors to write code, and IDEs (Integrated Development Environments, e.g. IDLE, Spyder) that combine editor, interpreter/compiler and debugger.

example.q: A program has errors on line 3 and line 7. What happens with an interpreter and with a compiler?
steps: Interpreter: runs lines 1 and 2, stops at line 3 and reports that error
Fix line 3, run again; it stops at line 7
Compiler: scans the whole program first and reports errors on lines 3 and 7 together
No machine code is produced until all errors are fixed
example.answer: Interpreter stops at the first error; compiler lists all errors after scanning the whole program.

learn.reallife: When you plug a new printer into a school lab PC, Windows installs its device driver. And the Python you'll write in this course runs through an interpreter like IDLE.

learn.hook: Your school's fee portal was built just for your school, but the browser you open it in is used by millions. Same 'app' word, very different software.
points: Application software helps users do specific tasks. General-purpose application software is ready-made for many users: word processors, spreadsheets, presentation tools, web browsers, image editors.
Customised (specific-purpose) software is built for one organisation's needs: a school's fee management system, a company's payroll, a railway reservation system.
Proprietary software: owned by a company; you buy a licence to use it and cannot see or change the source code (e.g. Microsoft Windows, MS Office).
Free and Open Source Software (FOSS): source code is available to view, modify and share (e.g. Linux/Ubuntu, Python, LibreOffice, Mozilla Firefox).
Freeware is free of cost, but its source code is not open; you can use it but not modify it. 'Free' in FOSS means freedom, not just zero price.

example.answer: General-purpose: Writer, Excel; customised: hospital system; FOSS: LibreOffice, Python; proprietary: Excel

learn.hook: You say 'Hey, call Mumma' and your phone dials. You never talk to the hardware; the operating system does it for you.
points: An operating system (OS) is system software that acts as an interface between the user and the hardware and manages all resources (CPU, memory, files, devices). Examples: Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS.

User interfaces: command-based (typing commands, e.g. MS-DOS, Linux terminal), GUI (icons, windows, menus), touch-based (smartphones, tablets), voice-based (voice assistants) and gesture-based (hand movements, e.g. some smart TVs, phones).
Process management: decides which program (process) gets the CPU and for how long. Memory management: allocates and frees primary memory for programs.
File management: creating, naming, organising, opening and deleting files and folders. Device management: controls I/O devices through drivers.
Common exam pairs: RAM vs ROM, compiler vs interpreter, system vs application software, data/address/control bus, and memory unit conversions.

example.q: You open a music app and a browser together, and copy a photo to a pen drive. Which OS functions are at work?
steps: Sharing the CPU between the two apps → process management
Giving each app its own space in RAM → memory management
Copying the photo and creating its entry on the pen drive → file management
Talking to the USB pen drive via its driver → device management
example.answer: Process, memory, file and device management

quiz.q: Which OS function decides which running program gets the CPU next?
quiz.explain: Scheduling programs on the CPU is process management.
steps: Choosing which running program gets the CPU next
is scheduling
That is process management
Answer: Process management
quiz.mistake: Confuses scheduling programs with managing memory

quiz.q: Allocating RAM to a newly opened app and freeing it when the app closes is:
quiz.explain: Handling primary memory space is the job of memory management.
steps: Giving RAM to a new app and freeing it when the app closes
is handling primary memory
That is memory management
Answer: Memory management
quiz.mistake: Thinks file management handles RAM

quiz.q: A Linux user types 'ls' to list files. Which type of interface is this?
quiz.explain: Typing text commands is a command-based (command-line) interface.
steps: The user types a text command, 'ls'
Typing text commands
is a command-based interface
Answer: Command-based
quiz.mistake: Thinks all Linux interfaces are graphical

quiz.q: Which is NOT an operating system?
quiz.explain: MS Word is an application (word processor); the others are operating systems.
steps: Linux, Android and Windows are operating systems
MS Word is a word processor, an application
So MS Word is NOT an operating system
Answer: MS Word
quiz.mistake: Thinks any well-known Microsoft product is an OS

quiz.q: Creating folders, naming files and controlling who may open them is part of:
quiz.explain: The OS's file system organises and protects files and folders.
steps: Creating folders, naming files and controlling access
is organising and protecting files
That is file management
Answer: File management
quiz.mistake: Mixes up file and memory management

quiz.q: Which statement is correct?
options: Both RAM and ROM are secondary memory
RAM is non-volatile and a compiler translates line by line
RAM is volatile, ROM is non-volatile; a compiler translates the whole program, an interpreter one line at a time
ROM is volatile and an interpreter translates the whole program
quiz.explain: This pairs the correct property with each memory and each translator.
steps: RAM is volatile and ROM is non-volatile
A compiler translates the whole program; an interpreter one line at a time
Only one option pairs all of these correctly
Answer: RAM is volatile, ROM is non-volatile; a compiler translates the whole program, an interpreter one line at a time
quiz.mistake: Swaps the properties within a pair

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A user can work on a computer without knowing how its hardware works.
Reason (R): The operating system provides an interface that hides hardware details.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because the OS hides the hardware behind a friendly interface, users don't need hardware knowledge.
steps: A: users can work without knowing how hardware works — true
R: the OS provides an interface that hides hardware details — true, and it explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Misses the link between the OS interface and ease of use

teach.ask: Gappu asks, 'What does an operating system actually do?' Explain the OS, its interfaces and its main functions.
teach.praise: The OS is my phone's manager — it juggles processes, memory, files and devices. Thank you!
teach.nudge: Nice. Which four things does the OS manage, and what does 'interface' mean here?

revise.summary: The operating system is system software that is the interface between user and hardware and manages resources. Interfaces can be command-based, GUI, touch, voice or gesture. Its functions are process, memory, file and device management.
focus: Define the OS and name examples
Identify types of user interface
Match tasks to process, memory, file and device management
remember: OS: interface between user and hardware; manages CPU, memory, files and devices
Interfaces: command-based, GUI, touch-based, voice-based, gesture-based
Process management: which program gets the CPU; memory management: allocating and freeing RAM
File management: creating, naming, organising files; device management: I/O through drivers
traps: MS Word is an application, not an operating system
Typing commands like 'ls' is a command-based interface, not a GUI
